text: Midsummer lies golden on the Pelennor — hay high in the fields, bees in the linden-rows, and the City walls shining in the long light. The orchards hang heavy and the dykes run slow and green.
The beacon-hills stand grey and bare; the high pastures are stiff with frost and the signal-wood is stacked dark against the sky. On clear days the whole line of peaks burns white to the south.
The fir-woods on the foothills stand black and quiet under a weight of frost. The snow creaks under the boughs and the resin-smell is sharp and cold.
Rain falls soft on the green townlands; the West Road shines wet and the beacon-hills are dim islands in the mist. The orchards drip and the fields drink.
Snow lies deep on the foothill pastures and the pine-woods carry it in white folds. The streams run dark and loud between icy banks.
Rain on the Pelennor is warm and fruitful; the dykes run full, the orchards shine, and the City stands grey-gold through the veil.
Cold comes down the mountain paths at dusk; the beacon-tops are icy and the air off the high snows bites the hands that tend the warning-fires.
The White Mountains are a frozen wall; their snow reaches down into the fir-woods, and Mindolluin stands over the City like the king of winter.
Winter seas are iron and slate; the wind is a great cold wheel out of the west, and the waves march in grey ranks to break upon the shores of Middle-earth.
Rain and sea-mist meet over the water; the horizon drowns, and the world becomes a grey wheel of wind and wet with no edge and no end.
The coast-lanes in winter are ways of white water and screaming wind; the seabirds hang like blown rags and the shore is a line of foam.
Rain flattens the grey water into a beaten sheet; the coast dissolves in mist, and sea and sky are one weeping grey.
The Chetwood stands bare and brown, its branches nearly stripped; an east wind seethes through it and brings cold rain down off the hills.
A curtain of rain hides Bree Hill, and the thatched roofs of the village shine dark with wet. Lights show early in the windows along the climbing street.
Rain falls without cease on the marshes; the pools spread and merge, the reeds stand black and dripping, and the cries of hidden birds come thin and mournful through the wet.
A chill hangs on the marsh water; mist clings to the reed-beds and the pools are rimmed with grey ice. The midges are gone, but a colder quiet has taken their place.
Rain drives down the East Road in gusts and the crossing ways shine like shallow streams. The Greenway northward is a drowned ribbon of grass.
The East Road lies hard and pale under frost; the Greenway's grass is stiff and whitened. Few travel, and the sky above the ridge is iron-grey.
Rain curtains the view across the River; the reeds bow, the pools blur into one grey sheet, and the far bank is a rumour and a shadow.
On the treeless plain the sun climbs to noon over waving grass; thin clouds drift up from the south and shadows lengthen across the open ground.
The wooded banks stand black and bare; mist lies along the pale margins of the water at dusk, and the rocks cast long shadows under a cold sky.
The River runs dark and high between its banks; mist lies on the water at dusk, and a cold wind follows the channel south.
Rain curtains the River; mist hides the far bank, and the channel narrows and quickens between steep grey shores until the rapids' roar comes up through the wet.
An icy morning wind moves over the plains; the stars fade on a pale eastern sky, and the grass crackles underfoot in the growing grey light.
Snow and storm rule the heights; ice falls like rain and the peaks vanish in a white fury that no traveller outfaces. The mountain itself seems to breathe malice.
Above the cloud-line the cold is absolute — fierce sunlight on a hard summit beneath a turning sky, thin air, and the slow groan of burdened stones.
Mountain storms fill the night with sudden flashes and thunder rolling through the hollows; the ledges stream with water and the valleys below are lost in murk.
Rain drives across the slopes and turns every ledge to a waterfall; the pines bend and hiss under the weight of it, and the paths are running mud.
Winter locks the passes: the trails are deep in drifted snow, the ice on the stones is glass-hard and deadly, and the way is memory and guesswork.
The middle slopes are buried in white silence; the pines carry it in great folds and the streams are frozen threads under the drifts.
The meres skin over with grey ice and the mist lies low and heavy; the pale lights still move over the pools, cold flames in a colder land.
Rain spreads the meres and drowns the causeways; the whole fen becomes a sheet of dark water, and the dead lie deeper and nearer.
The sun beats on the slag-mounds and the pits give back the heat; fumes rise, the air trembles, and the land sweats its poison.
The plain lies hard and black under frost; dust drives before the wind like dirty snow, and the mounds stand stark in the pale light.
The pale roads lie frozen, dust-dry and hard under the cold sky, leading on to the Gate — and there is no shelter anywhere along them.
The fen-paths are a cruel riddle of ice and water; every step breaks through to cold black mud, and the mist clings like a damp hand.
Snow lies on the young woods and the Mountain's flanks; the valley is white and still, and the ravens croak on the bare ridge above the gate.
Rain sweeps the long valley; the young pines shine dark and the grey scars of the old desolation run with black water.
The stony paths are white lines between black rocks; the wind off the Mountain is bitter, and the heights above are deep in drifted snow.
The road to the Gate runs white and cold beside the ice-rimmed river; the Mountain's peak stands over it like a white crown on a grey throne.
Snow fills the ravines and hides the paths; the broken slopes about the Mountain are a white maze of rock and drift.
The young woods are green and loud with birds; the Mountain's shadow lies cool across the valley floor, and the river runs bright between the banks.
The pines stand black and heavy under frost; the wood is very still, and breath smokes in air that smells of resin and cold earth.
Rain hisses in the pine-tops and runs in dark threads down the trunks; the forest floor drinks it in silence, and the air is green and dripping.
A deep cold pools under the pines; the moss is stiff and the old carved stones are white with rime.
Summer light reaches the old slabs in thin green shafts; the forest breathes warm and slow around the forgotten road.
The paths are black streams beneath the pines; the resin drips and the wood smells of wet needles and hidden watching.
The downs are brown and bare; the wind out of the Gap is keen, and the hill-steads send up thin grey smoke against the cold.
The stump-dotted hills stand black under frost; what woods remain are dark and still, and the land is bitter and bare.
Rain sweeps the Gap and the old road runs wet under the mountains' wall; the Isen comes down loud and brown and the fords run deep.
The hill-paths are rivulets; rain drives across the empty downs and the secret ways are grey threads in the wet.
Snow lies deep on the foothills and the gorges of the Isen are white; the passes above are closed and silent.
A hard cold sits on Dunland; the smoke of the stead-fires lies flat, and the wind off Methedras is a whetted edge.
The green woods stand dark and wet under the sea-wind; frost is rare here, but the rain of the western winter is long and cold.
Snow lies on the blue ridges and the gulf-wind is bitter; the Sea below is grey as iron and the hills are white above it.
Snow lies long on the high moors; the blue stone shows through it in bands, and the wind off the Sea is edged with ice.
The road to the Havens runs under a grey sky beside a grey gulf; the mountains are white above and the water dark below, and the way feels like the last way in the world.
Sea-rain drives across the ridges; the old paths run with water, and the mountains are a blue wall hidden in grey mist.
Rain comes in off the Sea in long veils; the woods drip and the mosses drink, and the air smells of salt and wet pine.
A cold clear dawn reveals the holly-hills crowned with dark leaves and red berries, and the snowy mountain-peaks stand ahead beyond them. The wind drops and the land holds its breath.
Snow lies on the high ridges of Eregion and clouds blow low across the passes. The holly shows black against the white slopes and the land is silent.
The wind drops and shifts at dawn and the cold is sharp and clear; every stone casts a blue shadow, and the air smells of the high snows.
The old road is a pale line under frost; the holly-berries are the only red thing in a white and silent land, and the mountains ahead are walls of winter.
Rain sweeps over the bare ridges and runs in the dry courses of the streams; for an hour the dead land drinks, then is barren and silent again.
Snow lies on the pines above the lake and the shores are rimmed with ice; the Long Lake is grey steel under white hills.
The channels skin with ice at the lake's edge; the town's lanterns reflect on black water and the wooden ways creak and sway in the cold.
The marsh-paths are frozen mud; the reeds are dead and white, and the lake-wind comes across the open water like a blade.
Rain mists the pines and raises the lake; the southern arms spread over their margins and the marsh-paths drown under brown water.
Rain beats on the lake and the wooden town; the channels blur, the lanterns halo in the wet, and the water rises around the piles.
Rain passes over the eaves almost unheard; beneath them is only the slow drip and the deep smell of wet leaf-mould. The forest drinks, and considers.
Snow lies on the eaves but under the boughs the air is cool rather than cold; the leaf-drifts are deep and soft, and the forest dreams of spring with open eyes.
Under the summer canopy the air is green, still and warm; shafts of sun come down like gold pillars, and the tree-shadows are cool pools on the leaves.
The paths are hidden under leaf and drifted snow; the forest holds its cold in stillness, and the high slopes are white and bare.
Cold in Fangorn is a deep slow thing — it sits in the leaf-drifts and the still air, old as the roots and patient as the shepherds.
Cold seeps out of the Vale; the white pinnacles are sharp in the freezing air, and the stream below steams like a breath in the cold.
The hills stand bare and colourless; ice rims the pools of the Morgulduin and the dead white flowers nod in the cold meadows.
The pale woods drip with cold dew; the leaves hang limp and black, and the Morgul-mist creeps among the trunks like a living thing.
Rain falls thin and cold on the haunted road; the carved king's crown of flowers is beaten down with wet, and the white stone glistens.
Ice glazes the narrow stairs; the crevices hold old snow, and the red glow above is blurred by cold mist.
Soft rain falls on the herb-glades and the resinous woods; the air is washed and sweet, and every bush drips with a sharper scent.
The gorse blazes gold on the warm hillsides; the sun draws up the smell of thyme and cedar, and the whole land hums with bees.
The glades are grey and the heath is bent low; frost lies in the sheltered hollows, but the air keeps a memory of herbs.
The South Road lies pale and empty under a cold sky; frost whitens its verges and the woods stand black along its edges.
The hidden paths run soft and wet; rain patters on the gorse, and the herbs give up their scent to the wet air.
The black trees of the Dimholt are rimed and still; frost fills the hollow between the ancient stones, and the dark beyond the door seems to breathe the cold.
Snow lies on the high pastures and the vale runs grey beneath it; lights begin to flicker early in the dwellings below.
Snow fills the spurs and the sheep-paths vanish; the dark firs of the Dimholt carry it in heavy black folds.
Rain falls grey on the vale and the Morthond rises dark and fast; the cliffs run with thin silver threads of water.
A cold comes down off the high snows and pools in the upper vale; the paths are white with frost and the black wood is silent.
The high peaks are a wall of winter; their snow reaches down to the black wood, and the vale below is a grey pool of dusk.
Grey clouds obscure the sun and the wind rises; willows bend and sigh beside swollen streams that rush down dark from the northern hills.
The downs lie white and lifeless under frost; the wind has the whole width of Eriador to gather speed in, and it does not spare the traveller.
Rain drives along the Road in long veils and the sky is the colour of the wet earth; after the storm the clouds break and a wandering moon rides over the drowned country.
The Road lies empty under a low grey sky; ice skins the puddles in its ruts, and there is no shelter from the wind for a mile in any direction.
Rain whispers in the thin woods and drips from bare alder twigs; the ground under the trees is black and soft and smells of rot.
A gentle rain passes over the Golden Wood and leaves everything fresh and clean; the air beneath the trees is sweet, and the gold leaves hold the light like lamps after rain.
In winter the mallorn-leaves turn pale gold and do not fall; the treetop air is cold, but the heart of the wood keeps a breath of spring.
Winter lies outside the fences, but the paths of Lórien run under gold boughs in air that is cool and sweet; winter here is a memory of elsewhere.
Sunlight falls through the high mallorn leaves in shafts of green and gold; elanor and niphredil star the grass of the clearings.
The paths are warm underfoot and the light is long; the Golden Wood in summer is a realm outside of time, dreaming in amber and green.
In summer the heat under the canopy is still and heavy, the air rank with spores; no breeze reaches through the interlaced boughs.
In winter the cold seeps up from the roots and frost makes strange patterns in the gloom; the black trunks stand bare and the dimness turns grey.
Rain on the eaves becomes a ceaseless drip below; the trunks run black with wet and the dim green light sinks to darkness.
Rain darkens the path to a black thread; the wood closes over it like a tunnel, and the drip of the trees is the only sound.
The false trails are drifts of black leaves gone stiff with frost; the dark stream is rimed at its edges and the wood is utterly still.
The cold in the deep wood is a damp, creeping thing — it lives in the black earth and the still air, and no fire built here burns right.
The beech-woods stand silver and bare; the great doors are shut against the cold, and the fires burn deep under the hill.
Rain on the north-eaves is a green dripping; the Forest River runs full and dark under its bridge, and the air smells of wet earth and old stone.
Snow lies on the paths to the doors; the deer come down to the frozen river-meadows, and the wood is white and silent.
The green wood is loud with birdsong; feasts in the torch-lit glades go on into the long twilight, and lanterns move like stars under the leaves.
Snow closes over the Dimrill Dale and the Stair; the passes fill with drifting white, and the peaks above are lost in storm.
On the high slopes the snow falls thick and blinding; the wind heaps it in the clefts, and the mountain seems to breathe a white malice.
The cold on Caradhras is beyond frost and wind; it is a hatred in the stone itself, and no fire at its feet will warm it.
Rain fills the empty stream-beds for an hour and the hills run with sudden water; then the channels fall silent and red-stained again.
Winter wraps the Dale in deep snow and Mirrormere lies black and still, reflecting only the stars and the shoulders of the peaks.
The trail to the Stair vanishes under drifted snow; the way is memory and guesswork between white walls of stone.
The heat comes off the plain in waves; the ash-shimmer hides the distances and the fume of Orodruin hangs red and heavy. Thirst is a torment here.
Winter in Gorgoroth is a cold more bitter than the heat — black frost on the slag, and wind off the mountains that cuts through every rag.
Cold pools in the ravines of the Morgai; the scree is stiff with frost and the jagged ridges ring in the freezing air.
The roads bake under the dim red sun; dust rises from the marching columns and the iron ruts shine like heated wire.
The dust lies frozen in the ruts; the way is iron-hard and the cold wind drives black sleet across the empty miles.
The ravine-paths are fanged with black ice; the cold climbs out of the depths and the stone bites the hand that holds it.
When rain comes to the inner country it falls black and hot through the fumes; the ash turns to black mud and the thorn-brakes steam.
The oaks stand bare and the mast lies deep under the leaves; frost whitens the ford-stones and the River runs dark and cold.
The Gladden Fields lie silent under frost — brown reeds, black pools, and the thin cry of a single bird over the wide water.
Rain swells the ford until the stepping-stones run just awash; the mountains hide behind grey cloud and the River is loud between the banks.
Snow fills the vales and caps the Carrock like a white crown; the trails are a single white line between the River and the black eaves of Mirkwood.
The vales are loud with bees; the oakwoods are deep green, and the high grass of the meadows stands ready for the scythe.
The northern peaks stand deep in winter long after the vales are green; avalanches growl in the gullies, and the passes are a white silence.
Cold rules the heights; even the eagles keep their eyries close, and the wind off the ice-fields numbs the air it touches.
Storms rake the high slopes; water pours off the crags in silver threads, and the caves of the pass drip and echo.
Rain brings the hillsides down in wet cascades; the paths to the pass are running streams, and the shelters of the rocks are black with damp.
The winter paths are buried; the way is marked only by the line of the crags, and wolves follow what the snow conceals.
Rain sifts down through the close leaves in a fine cold drizzle; every trunk glistens black and the drip of water fills the silence. The wood seems pleased, and deepens around the path.
Even at midsummer the heat dies at the eaves; within, the air is green, dim and cool, smelling of leaf-mould and damp bark.
Bare black branches net the grey sky, and the floor is a drift of wet leaves over hidden roots. The cold seeps upward like a held breath.
Frost finds little purchase under the boughs, but a damp chill works through cloth and leather alike; the mist of the valley clings cold to the skin.
The old path is a mire of half-frozen leaves; the trees crowd closer in the pale light, and the way seems shorter each time it is sought.
The field lies bare and brown; the wind comes down off the mountains with ice in it, and the grass is stiff with frost.
Rain sweeps the open field; the grass lies flat and shining, and the old mounds stand dark in the wet.
The groves stand leafless and the brown drifts of mast lie deep; the paths are silent but for the drip of the thaw.
The road-line lies under summer grass and flowers; larksong is everywhere and the field is a green sea moving in the wind.
The green ways are hard under frost; the air is keen and the view to the mountains is bright and cold as drawn steel.
An east wind streams through bare branches and seethes in the dark pines beneath low, ragged clouds; the river roars among the stones, and the grey of December lies on the moor.
The pines seethe and sigh under a streaming east wind; below in the valley the sheltered boughs hold their green, and the sound of the falls comes up muffled through the cold.
A westerly wind brings cold rain through the hills, driving the last yellow leaves across the path; below, the Bruinen runs loud and wild and mist closes over the valley mouth.
Cold rain slants down the moor and turns the stony way to a shining thread; in the valley the river's voice swells until the hills ring with it.
The warm evening air smells of trees and flowers; running water sounds in the valley below, and it seems that summer lingers here beyond its time.
Golden light lies long on the valley woods; the Bruinen murmurs under the eaves, and the air is sweet with leaf and bloom.
The plains lie pale and sere under the winter sky; a thin searching wind comes down off the northern snows, and the grass is grey as the manes of horses.
The grassland stands high and green-gold; the wind moves through it like a tide, and larks sing invisible in the warm blue air.
Rain sweeps the open Mark in long grey veils; the grass lies flat and shining, and the horizon is a wall of moving water.
A keen cold rides the plains; the wind out of the north comes unhindered across a hundred miles of frozen grass.
Snow lies on the green foothills and the dales are white between black fir-woods; the Snowbourn runs dark and loud under icy banks.
The White Mountains stand to their waists in snow; the high pastures are buried, and the wind off the peaks brings ice-dust down to the dales.
The road to Edoras lies pale and hard under frost; the green hill of Meduseld stands grey above it, and the Golden Hall's thatch is dull under the cold sky.
The hill-tracks are white lines in the sere grass; the dale-streams are rimed at their edges, and the high refuges are cold and empty.
The fir-woods of the dales stand black under snow; the wind seethes in them, and the green eaves of Fangorn's edge are dark and still.
Rain fills the springs and darkens the lawns; Rauros roars louder through the wet, and the mist of the falls mingles with low cloud.
A bitter east wind moves over the fens; the pools skin with ice at their edges, and the reeds hiss like steel.
The stone steps are slick with frost and the high seat stands cold and empty; below, the Falls thunder on regardless through the white land.
The fens spread and swell in the rain; every hollow is a pool, and mist and water make a single grey country.
The copses stand in deep leaf and the sound of bees comes out of the clover at their feet; sunlight lies in golden patches on the grass beneath the boughs.
The bare branches drip and the rides are drifts of sodden leaves; now and then a red berry shows on the holly, the only bright thing in the grey wood.
Snow lies along the hedgerows and the round doors in the hillsides look out on a white, quiet world; smoke climbs straight from hidden chimneys.
The meadows by the Water stand sheeted and shining, and the reeds bow under the weight of the rain; every ditch brims and hurries.
Rain sweeps across the open fields in grey curtains, pattering on fallen leaves and dimpling the puddles of the East Road; beyond the hedges the world is all wet gleam and running water.
Dust lies warm on the East Road and the hedgerows are loud with small birds; the way runs on golden and drowsy between the fields.
Frost whitens the narrow paths and the grass crackles underfoot; breath smokes on the still air between the bare hedges.
The tall woods stand leafless and dark against the white towers; the sea-wind brings a smell of salt up the western slopes.
The road west runs pale under frost; the towers stand white on the hill, and beyond them the Sea is grey and near.
Rain blows in off the unseen Sea; the green hills shine dark with wet and the towers are blurred above the streaming woods.
Rain sweeps the western slopes; the woods hiss and drip, and the towers stand dim white shapes in the murk.
Rain soaks the woods for days on end; fires will not kindle, and the dripping of the beeches goes on long after the sky has cleared.
Snow fills the hollows and the ravines; the stony paths are treacherous with ice, and the mountain wind drives flakes like ash through the trees.
The cold settles in the folds of the hills; even the streams run quieter, and the rock holds the frost long after noon.
The Road runs wet and gloomy under streaming skies; the fords rise brown and fast, and the stone of the hills shines black with wet.
Ice feathers the rocks beside the path and every breath smokes; the hollows below are pits of shadow and cold fern.
West winds drive fine, soaking rain onto the dark hills; the ridges run with water and the stones are black and streaming.
Snow lies thin and dirty on the northern slopes, and the wind off the high moor cuts like a drawn blade; the ruined walls give no shelter.
The cold comes down off the hills at dusk; sparse grass and withered leaves barely stir, and every hollow holds its own shadow and its own chill.
The thickets are brittle with frost and the grey grass is stiff underfoot; nothing moves in the scrub but the wind, searching.
Rain curtains the hills and turns the Road's verge to black mud; the land runs with whispering water, and the towers stand unseen in the murk.
The Wold lies sere and empty; frost whitens the long grass and the northern wind drives thin snow across the open downs.
A grey cold lies on the Wold; the land is a frozen sea of pale grass, and the dark of Fangorn is a black wall on the horizon.
The birch-woods stand white and bare; the tracks are lost in drifted grass, and the dark line of Fangorn is blurred by falling snow.
The green tracks are hard under frost; the way north is an empty line between white field and grey sky.
Rain drives over the open downs; the grass-tracks run with water and the mist hides the dark eaves of the forest to the east.
The oaks stand bare and the mast lies deep under frost; the clearings are white, and the smoke of the hidden halls climbs into the cold.
Rain drips through the eaves and pools on the paths; the wood smells of wet leaf and hidden smoke, and the deer stand still in the oak-shelter.
The woods are deep green and loud with bees; the meadows of the clearings stand high with grass, and the air is warm and sweet.
The paths are drifts of leaves frozen hard; the marks of the Woodmen are sharp in the frost and the deer have gone to the sheltered glades.
